angle: confession: things that are shocking or illegal today
title: I'm 82. What Doctors Did to Us in the 1950s Would Be ILLEGAL Today

scenes.text: Sweetheart, when you had that ear infection last month, your mother drove you to the urgent care, and they looked it up on a computer, and they gave you exactly the right medicine. I sat in the waiting room thinking, if only my mother could see this. Because when I was a little girl in the nineteen fifties, sweetheart, some of what the doctors did to us would get them arrested today.
scenes.caption: IF MY MOTHER COULD SEE THIS

scenes.text: I'm not saying they were bad men. Most of them were kind, and they worked themselves to death. They just didn't know what we know now. And some things they did know, and did anyway, because that's how it was done. So let me tell you, one by one. Some of these will make you laugh. A few of them won't.
scenes.caption: ONE BY ONE

scenes.text: Number one. Our family doctor, Dr. Hartman, smoked in the examining room. With me sitting on the table in my undershirt. He'd listen to my chest with his stethoscope and a Lucky Strike in the corner of his mouth, and the ash would get longer and longer, and I would just watch that ash, waiting for it to fall on me. It never did. He was an expert.
scenes.caption: A LUCKY STRIKE

scenes.text: And you know why nobody thought that was strange? Because the cigarette companies put doctors in their advertising. More doctors smoke Camels than any other cigarette, it said, in every magazine in our house. There was a man in a white coat, smiling, with a cigarette. My father switched to Camels because of that ad. He thought it was the healthy choice.
scenes.caption: MORE DOCTORS SMOKE CAMELS

scenes.text: The Surgeon General didn't say smoking causes cancer until January of nineteen sixty-four. By then my father had been smoking for twenty-five years. In our house there was an ashtray in every room, even the bathroom. And when I had a cough as a little girl, sweetheart, nobody told my father to put it out. They just told me to drink more water.
scenes.caption: AN ASHTRAY IN EVERY ROOM

scenes.text: Number two, and this one's true, I promise. When you went to buy shoes at the shoe store downtown, they had a big wooden machine, like a cabinet, called a fluoroscope. You stood on a step and put your feet in a slot at the bottom, and you looked through a little window at the top. And you could see the bones of your toes, wiggling, inside your new shoes. It was an X-ray machine.
scenes.caption: THE SHOE FITTING MACHINE

scenes.text: There was no lead apron. Nobody timed it. Danny and I would stand there for minutes at a time, wiggling our toes and giggling, while my mother talked to the salesman. Some children went back every week just to play with it. There were thousands of those machines in shoe stores all over America. By the end of the fifties, states started banning them, one by one. Now you know why.
scenes.caption: NO LEAD APRON

scenes.text: Number three. When Danny was teething, my mother rubbed his gums with something called paregoric. It came from the drugstore in a little brown bottle. You know what paregoric was, sweetheart? It was made with opium. Opium, for babies. And it worked, oh, it worked. Danny would fall asleep in two minutes, smiling.
scenes.caption: A LITTLE BROWN BOTTLE

scenes.text: And for a cough, Grandma Pearl swore by cough syrup with codeine in it. In Ohio, in those years, you could buy some codeine cough syrups without a prescription. You just signed a book at the pharmacy counter. My mother signed that book every winter. Nobody thought of it as a drug. It was just what you had in the cupboard, next to the Vicks.
scenes.caption: SIGN THE BOOK

scenes.text: For a scraped knee, it was Mercurochrome, that bright red stuff that stung like fire and stained your skin for a week. Every child in America had red knees in the summer. It was made with mercury. Years and years later the government decided it wasn't safe after all. I've still got a little bottle somewhere. I'll show you. Don't touch it.
scenes.caption: RED KNEES

scenes.text: Number four. This is the one that scares me now. In the summer, to kill the mosquitoes, a truck came down our street at dusk, spraying a big white cloud out of the back. A fogging truck. It was DDT. And do you know what we children did? We ran behind it. Every kid on Elm Street, on our bicycles, riding right into the fog, because it was cool and it smelled sweet.
scenes.caption: WE RAN BEHIND IT

scenes.text: Our mothers didn't call us in. They thought it was good for us. No mosquitoes, no disease. They sprayed DDT on beaches with children playing, on cows, on kitchen walls. There were advertisements with a happy housewife and a cartoon bug. Then in nineteen sixty-two a woman named Rachel Carson wrote a book called Silent Spring. And ten years later, in nineteen seventy-two, DDT was banned.
scenes.caption: SILENT SPRING

scenes.text: Number five. Having a baby. When my mother had Danny in nineteen forty-seven, my father wasn't allowed in the delivery room. Fathers never were. They sat in a waiting room down the hall, smoking, with the other fathers, for hours. A nurse came out and said, it's a boy, Mr. Miller, and he handed out cigars. That's all a father did.
scenes.caption: IT'S A BOY

scenes.text: And the mothers, sweetheart. Many hospitals gave women something called twilight sleep. A shot that made you forget. You'd wake up hours later and they'd bring you a baby, and you didn't remember a thing. Some women were tied to the bed so they wouldn't hurt themselves while they were under. My mother told me this only once, when she was very old. She didn't want to talk about it again.
scenes.caption: TWILIGHT SLEEP

scenes.text: Then they kept you in the hospital a week or more, flat on your back. And the babies were kept in a nursery behind a glass window, in rows. The fathers would come and look at them through the glass, and the mothers saw them every four hours, on schedule, for feeding. Not one minute early, even if the baby was crying. That was the rule.
scenes.caption: BEHIND THE GLASS

scenes.text: Number six. Every child had their tonsils out. Every single one. Sore throat twice in one winter? Out they come. I had mine out when I was six, at Mansfield General. They put a rubber mask over my face that smelled like ether, a sweet, sick smell, and told me to count backwards from ten. I got to seven.
scenes.caption: COUNT BACKWARDS FROM TEN

scenes.text: When I woke up, my throat felt like I'd swallowed a cactus, and the nurse gave me a bowl of ice cream. That was the best part. All the children in the ward were eating ice cream. Today, sweetheart, doctors hardly ever take tonsils out, unless they really have to. Back then, they took out millions of them a year. Mine were perfectly fine, I found out later.
scenes.caption: THE ICE CREAM

scenes.text: And here's the part that broke my heart. While I was in that hospital, my mother could only visit me for one hour a day. Visiting hours, they called it, from two to three. Some hospitals let parents see their children only on Sundays. They said seeing the mothers made the children cry more. So you lay there at night, six years old, in a room full of strangers, and you cried anyway.
scenes.caption: TWO TO THREE

scenes.text: Now, I'll tell you one thing that was better. House calls. If you were too sick to go out, the doctor came to you. Dr. Hartman came up our front walk with his black leather bag, in the snow, at nine o'clock at night. He sat on my bed, felt my forehead, gave me a shot of penicillin right there, and charged my father five dollars. Then he had a cup of coffee in the kitchen.
scenes.caption: FIVE DOLLARS

scenes.text: Penicillin was still new, you see. It had only been in drugstores since after the war. And doctors gave it for everything, a cold, a sore throat, whatever you had. A shot in the behind with a big glass syringe, which they boiled on the stove to clean. Not thrown away. Boiled and used again, on the next patient.
scenes.caption: BOILED ON THE STOVE

scenes.text: And now the one that isn't funny. Polio. Every summer when I was a child, our mothers were terrified. Polio was a virus that could paralyze a child in a few days. Nobody knew exactly how it spread. So in July and August, they closed the swimming pools. They closed the movie theaters to children. My mother wouldn't let us drink from a water fountain.
scenes.caption: THE POOLS CLOSED

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-two, the worst year, there were fifty-seven thousand cases in America. Children in iron lungs, big metal tubes that breathed for them, in long rows in the hospital. A boy in my second-grade class went in one August and never came back to school. We didn't talk about it. We just looked at his empty desk.
scenes.caption: 57,000 CASES

scenes.text: Then on the twelfth of April, nineteen fifty-five, they announced on the radio that Dr. Jonas Salk's vaccine worked. Church bells rang. People cried in the street. Two weeks later they lined us up in the school gymnasium for the shot. I've never seen a line of children so happy to get a needle in their arm.
scenes.caption: APRIL 12, 1955

scenes.text: But even that had a dark side, sweetheart. One company, Cutter Laboratories, made a bad batch. Some of their vaccine had live virus in it. Tens of thousands of children got sick from it, and some of them died or were paralyzed. After that, the government made the rules much stricter. A lot of today's rules were written because of a mistake like that.
scenes.caption: THE CUTTER BATCH

scenes.text: And when I was sixteen, my friend Carol went to a doctor because she thought she was too heavy for her prom dress. She wasn't, sweetheart, she was a stick. He gave her a bottle of little pills to take every morning. Diet pills. They were amphetamines. She cleaned her whole house at midnight and couldn't sleep for a month. Doctors handed those out like candy, to girls, to housewives, to anybody.
scenes.caption: LITTLE PILLS

scenes.text: And one last story. Around nineteen sixty, a German company had a sleeping pill called thalidomide. Doctors in Europe gave it to pregnant women for morning sickness. And an American company wanted to sell it here too. It was almost on the shelves. One woman stopped it. A doctor at the Food and Drug Administration named Frances Kelsey.
scenes.caption: ONE WOMAN SAID NO

scenes.text: She said the company hadn't proven it was safe, and she kept saying no, for more than a year, while they pressured her. And then the news came from Europe. Thousands of babies were being born with terrible problems, because their mothers took that pill. President Kennedy gave Dr. Kelsey a medal in nineteen sixty-two. American mothers like me owe her more than we can say.
scenes.query: 1962 Kennedy presents award ceremony White House
scenes.caption: A MEDAL FROM THE PRESIDENT

scenes.text: So, sweetheart, that's how it was. Smoking doctors, X-ray shoe machines, opium for babies and DDT for dessert. We survived most of it, but not everybody did. So next time you complain about all the warnings on a medicine bottle, remember, every one of those warnings is there because somebody, somewhere, learned the hard way.
scenes.caption: WE LEARNED THE HARD WAY

scenes.text: Now tell me in the comments. Did your shoe store have one of those X-ray machines? Did you run behind the fogging truck? I want to know I wasn't the only one. Goodnight, sweetheart. Grandma Ruth will be right here with another story tomorrow.
scenes.caption: DID YOU RUN BEHIND IT?
